newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parliament set to vote on pension funds.
newsitem.headline: French parliament set to vote on pension funds.

text.p: The French parliament was expected on Thursday or Friday to back a bill setting up retirement savings plans, ending years of debate on the merits of bringing Anglo-Saxon style pension funds to France.
Parliamentarian Jean-Pierre Thomas, who sponsored a bill on pension funds, expected parliamentary approval either at the end of a debate on Thursday, or on Friday at the latest.
"We will not leave this assembly with a text which has not been voted through. At the worst it will be Friday morning," he told Reuters.
Government officials and members of parliament were still working out last-minute amendments to the bill late on Wednesday and declined all comment on its contents.
But sources close to the talks said the plan was to allow pension funds to make up to 20 percent of their payouts in a lump sum with the bulk to be paid out in the form of annuities.

The Finance Ministry originally had suggested that pension funds make payouts in annuities only, but it ran into flak from Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who said the funds should be allowed to make payouts in capital in some cases.
"The prime minister wanted payouts in capital. So there will be payouts in capital," one source said.

The compromise on capital payouts aimed to end a debate which has pitted insurance companies, which favoured payouts in annuities, against banks, which argued that people should be able to choose to take their money in capital.
The sources said there would be a limit on the amount in francs that could be taken out in a lump sum, but said the figure had not been decided.
The funds, which will be set up through a joint agreement between employers and employees, will be managed independently by insurers, banks or mutual groups.
The bill was likely to stipulate the funds could invest a maximum of around 60 percent of their assets in bonds, the sources said.

Members of parliament originally insisted the funds must invest a minimum of their assets in shares to boost French companies share capital. But they were forced to drop the requirement to comply with European Union rules.
Employee contributions to pension funds are expected to be tax deductible, while payouts will be subject to income tax.

The sources said the government had still to decide whether employer contributions should be subject to payroll taxes used to fund the existing system of universal pensions. Such an exemption would lay it open to criticism of running down resources available for the existing pensions system.

Unlike Britain and the United States, where pension funds are huge stock market players, France depends on a system of universal pensions where the cost of paying pensioners is levied from the wages of today's workforce.
It has spent years discussing how such funds should be set up to complement the existing system, running at times into accusations from unions of privatising the welfare system.
The opposition Socialist party on Wednesday slammed the government's pension funds plans, calling them "a new step in the attack against the welfare system".
Financial markets are closely watching the debate on pension funds, particularly for any proposals that might affect the allocation of assets between stocks and bonds.
